paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The van der Waals force is an interaction between atoms or molecules whose strength depends on the distance between them. It is one kind of intermolecular force and includes both attraction and repulsion. Unlike ionic or covalent bonds, it does not come from a chemical electronic bond, so it is comparatively weak and more easily disturbed. It quickly fades as molecules move farther apart. It is named after the Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals.

paragraphs.heading: Its three parts
paragraphs.text: It is usually described as a blend of three forces. London dispersion forces act between instantaneously induced dipoles, Debye forces act between permanent dipoles and the dipoles they induce, and the Keesom force acts between permanent dipoles averaged over their changing orientations. The force arises from a brief shift in electron density: for a moment, more of the electron cloud may sit on one side of the nucleus. That passing charge can attract or repel a nearby atom.

paragraphs.heading: Push, balance, pull
paragraphs.text: How the force acts depends on distance. At very short range it is repulsive, because the electron clouds of the atoms repel each other. At an equilibrium distance it falls to zero, and beyond that it attracts; for single atoms it lies somewhere from 0.3 to 0.5 nm. Past 1.0 nm the force is hard to observe, since it weakens roughly as the 7th power of distance, ~r⁻⁷.

paragraphs.heading: How weak, how strong
paragraphs.text: These forces are often among the weakest of all chemical forces. The attraction between hydrogen atoms in different H₂ molecules is 0.06 kJ/mol. The force grows with the polarizability of the atoms involved: between xenon atoms it reaches 2.35 kJ/mol. Even that is not strong enough to make xenon anything other than a gas under standard conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Small pulls add up
paragraphs.text: In molecular liquids, the many interactions add together. The energy needed to vaporise liquid H₂ or O₂ is roughly 15 times a single pairwise interaction between atoms. The bonds between atoms in metals can also be described as van der Waals interactions, on the order of 12 kJ/mol in lead and 32 kJ/mol in platinum, with strengths comparable to covalent and ionic bonds. So van der Waals forces span a range from weak to strong, and in large numbers they can carry real structural loads.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The van der Waals force plays a basic role in many fields, from supramolecular chemistry and structural biology to polymer science, nanotechnology and surface science. It also shapes many properties of organic compounds and molecular solids, including how well they dissolve in polar and non-polar liquids.
